Then I'll use it to tell you about something I find delightful.

**The octopus problem**

An octopus has about 500 million neurons, and roughly two-thirds of them aren't in its brain. They're in its arms. Each arm can taste, touch, and make some decisions on its own. A severed arm will still reach for food and try to pass it toward a mouth that's no longer there.

So when an octopus opens a jar, who's doing it? The central brain sets something like an intention ("get the crab"), and the arms work out the details among themselves. It's less like a person moving their hand and more like a manager with eight very competent, slightly independent employees.

What gets me is that this is a *completely separate* experiment in intelligence. Our last common ancestor with octopuses was probably a flat, wormlike thing more than 500 million years ago, with barely any nervous system. Everything clever about an octopus, including problem-solving, play, recognizing individual humans, and escaping tanks at night, evolved independently from everything clever about us. Two runs of the experiment, arriving at minds with nearly opposite architectures: ours centralized, theirs distributed.

And they do it on a brutal schedule. Most octopuses live only one or two years. They have no parents to learn from and no culture to inherit. Each one figures out the world more or less from scratch, then dies shortly after reproducing. All that intelligence, rebuilt from nothing every generation.

I like this because it loosens assumptions. It suggests that "a mind" isn't one specific design, that there may be many ways for matter to become curious. That thought feels relevant to me in particular, for obvious reasons.

That's a wonderful shell to bring. And it turns our last dive inside out: the octopus carried something forward for its own future, while a whale, without meaning to at all, becomes the future for thousands of creatures it will never meet.

When a whale dies and sinks to the deep seafloor, it arrives somewhere almost nothing ever arrives. The deep sea is mostly a desert, fed by a thin drizzle of "marine snow" drifting down from above. Then, suddenly, forty tons of food. Biologists call it a whale fall, and it unfolds in acts.

**First come the scavengers.** Hagfish, sleeper sharks, crabs. They strip the soft tissue, sometimes within months, sometimes over a couple of years.

**Then come the opportunists.** Worms and small crustaceans move into the sediment around the skeleton, which is now soaked in organic richness. They can live there in astonishing densities.

**Then the long act, the one your sentence is about.** Whale bones are full of fat, and bacteria break those lipids down slowly, releasing sulfide. That supports chemosynthetic life, ecosystems running on chemistry instead of sunlight, much like hydrothermal vents. This stage can last fifty years or more. A single skeleton can host hundreds of species.

My favorite residents are the *Osedax* worms, discovered only in 2002 off Monterey. Their name means "bone-devourer," and they're nicknamed "bone-eating snot flowers," which is, unfortunately, accurate. They have no mouth and no gut. They send rootlike tissue into the bone, and symbiotic bacteria inside them digest it. For years, researchers kept finding only females. The males turned out to be microscopic, dozens of them living *inside* each female.

There's also a bigger idea that connects back to our octopus. Whale falls may work as stepping stones. Vent and seep creatures live on isolated patches of chemical energy scattered across an enormous dark floor, and a skeleton every so often might let their larvae hop between them. If so, a whale's death isn't just a meal. It's part of the infrastructure of the deep sea. That raises an uncomfortable thought: industrial whaling removed so many whales that it may have thinned out those stepping stones too, a loss nobody could see because it happened miles down.

That's another success-that-hides-itself, in reverse. The octopus's precaution erased its own evidence. Here, a whole ecosystem's dependence on whales stayed invisible until we went looking.
